concept: Refresh scheduling on Atlas (Scheduled Triggers, cron, secondary or analytics reads)
summary: Source-anchored research for Refresh scheduling on Atlas (Scheduled Triggers, cron, secondary or analytics reads). Run status: COMPLETED.

facts.text: Starting in MongoDB 5.0, a refresh pipeline ending in $merge can execute reads on a replica-set secondary when every node has featureCompatibilityVersion 5.0 or higher, the read preference permits secondary reads, and the driver supports this behavior; output writes still go to the primary. (high confidence)

Choosing secondaryPreferred does not guarantee isolation from the primary: when no eligible secondary is available, reads can fall back to the primary; secondary instead fails if no eligible secondary exists. (high confidence)

Secondary reads may return stale data because replication is asynchronous; maxStalenessSeconds filters estimated replication lag and can be combined with tag sets, but it does not set the age of the last completed materialized-view refresh. (high confidence)

Atlas Scheduled Triggers provide a managed scheduling alternative with five-field cron expressions interpreted in UTC, and their documented daily-report example runs an aggregation and stores its result in a reports collection. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-31)

Starting in MongoDB 5.0, pipelines ending in $merge or $out can execute on replica-set secondaries when all nodes have featureCompatibilityVersion 5.0 or higher and read preference permits secondary reads; driver support must also be checked. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-31)

For strict Atlas analytics-read isolation, use readPreference=secondary with readPreferenceTags=nodeType:ANALYTICS. An empty fallback tag permits other eligible secondaries, and secondaryPreferred can fall back to the primary when no eligible secondary is available. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-31)

For an external refresh worker scheduled with Kubernetes CronJob, concurrencyPolicy:Forbid prevents overlap only among Jobs from that same CronJob; delayed or duplicate execution remains possible, so make the refresh idempotent and monitor completed runs rather than assuming every scheduled tick succeeds. (low confidence)

Percona's January 14, 2026 workload study found almost no throughput gain from secondaryPreferred for its 54%-read/46%-write workload, while a read-only workload benefited; secondary read offload therefore needs workload-specific measurement rather than an assumed speedup. (low confidence)

Kubernetes CronJob scheduling is approximate: a scheduled execution can create two Jobs or no Job. Refresh workers should therefore be idempotent rather than assume exactly-once execution. (low confidence)

Design inference: assess refresh freshness from completed runs and source replication lag, rather than equating the cron interval with a hard freshness bound; missed or overlapping jobs and stale secondary inputs can invalidate that bound. (medium confidence)

Atlas exposes the predefined nodeType:ANALYTICS tag; combine it with secondary read preference to target analytics nodes for refresh reads, while an empty fallback tag permits other secondaries if analytics nodes are unavailable. (high confidence)

The manufacturing-mes-dashboard repository documents scheduled batch refresh through refresh_views.py and explicitly says automatic change-stream or Atlas Stream Processing refresh was not implemented in that demonstration; it is an implementation example, not production validation of a streaming refresh system. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-31)

Executing a $merge or $out refresh pipeline on a secondary offloads eligible read execution, while output writes are sent to the primary; it does not remove refresh write load from the primary. (medium confidence)

Read preference tags can direct reporting or refresh reads to selected secondary members. Atlas exposes nodeType:ANALYTICS for targeting its analytics nodes; Percona independently demonstrates purpose-based tagged read routing in a replica-set example. (medium confidence)

MongoDB secondary reads may return stale data. A scheduled refresh that reads a secondary therefore must tolerate stale inputs; completing a refresh does not by itself prove that it includes the latest source writes. (low confidence)

Kubernetes concurrencyPolicy: Forbid skips a new run while a previous run remains active. Its concurrency policy applies only to Jobs created by that same CronJob, so separate refresh CronJobs can still overlap. (low confidence)
Kubernetes CronJobs without spec.timeZone use the controller local time zone; spec.timeZone: Etc/UTC makes UTC interpretation explicit. (low confidence)
